claim: Profilin-1 (PFN1) is a cytoskeletal protein that regulates the dynamics of actin and microtubule assembly.
source: Profilin-1 (PFN1) is a cytoskeletal protein that regulates the dynamics of actin and microtubule assembly.
evidence: This is a general statement about PFN1 function that is supported by the subsequent experimental data and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: PFN1 is essential for the normal division, motility, and morphology of cells.
source: Thus, PFN1 is essential for the normal division, motility, and morphology of cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by the cell-based experiments showing morphological and cytoskeletal defects in PFN1-deficient cells (Figure 6).

claim: Conventional fusion and direct labeling strategies compromise different facets of PFN1 function.
source: Unfortunately, conventional fusion and direct labeling strategies compromise different facets of PFN1 function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and the rationale for developing new tagged versions.

claim: The only methods used to determine known PFN1 functions have been indirect and often deduced in cell-free biochemical assays.
source: As a consequence, the only methods used to determine known PFN1 functions have been indirect and often deduced in cell-free biochemical assays.
evidence: This is supported by the literature review in the introduction and citations to previous work.

claim: Two genetically encoded versions of tagged PFN1 (Halo-PFN1 and mApple-PFN1) behave identical to each other and the tag-free protein.
source: We engineered and characterized two genetically encoded versions of tagged PFN1 that behave identical to each other and the tag-free protein.
evidence: This is supported by multiple biochemical assays comparing tagged and untagged proteins (Figures 2-5).

claim: Purified mAp-PFN1 binds to phosphoinositide lipids.
source: In biochemical assays purified proteins bind to phosphoinositide lipids, catalyze nucleotide exchange on actin monomers, stimulate formin-mediated actin filament assembly, and bound tubulin dimers (kD = 1.89 µM) to impact microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by liposome pelleting assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Purified mAp-PFN1 catalyzes nucleotide exchange on actin monomers.
source: In biochemical assays purified proteins bind to phosphoinositide lipids, catalyze nucleotide exchange on actin monomers, stimulate formin-mediated actin filament assembly, and bound tubulin dimers (kD = 1.89 µM) to impact microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by time-resolved fluorescence polarization assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Purified mAp-PFN1 stimulates formin-mediated actin filament assembly.
source: In biochemical assays purified proteins bind to phosphoinositide lipids, catalyze nucleotide exchange on actin monomers, stimulate formin-mediated actin filament assembly, and bound tubulin dimers (kD = 1.89 µM) to impact microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by bulk fluorescence and TIRF microscopy assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: mAp-PFN1 bound tubulin dimers with a kD of 1.89 µM.
source: In biochemical assays purified proteins bind to phosphoinositide lipids, catalyze nucleotide exchange on actin monomers, stimulate formin-mediated actin filament assembly, and bound tubulin dimers (kD = 1.89 µM) to impact microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence polarization assays shown in Figure 5G.

claim: mAp-PFN1 impacts microtubule dynamics.
source: In biochemical assays purified proteins bind to phosphoinositide lipids, catalyze nucleotide exchange on actin monomers, stimulate formin-mediated actin filament assembly, and bound tubulin dimers (kD = 1.89 µM) to impact microtubule dynamics.
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy assays of microtubule polymerization shown in Figure 5.

claim: In PFN1-deficient mammalian cells, Halo-PFN1 or mApple-PFN1 restored morphological and cytoskeletal functions.
source: In PFN1-deficient mammalian cells, Halo-PFN1 or mApple-PFN1 (mAp-PEN1) restored morphological and cytoskeletal functions.
evidence: This is supported by cell morphology and cytoskeletal imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Titrations of self-labeling Halo-ligands were used to visualize molecules of PFN1.
source: Titrations of self-labeling Halo-ligands were used to visualize molecules of PFN1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the live-cell imaging experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: Function-disrupting point-mutants (Y6D and R88E) revealed PFN1 bound to microtubules in live cells.
source: This approach combined with specific function-disrupting point-mutants (Y6D and R88E) revealed PFN1 bound to microtubules in live cells.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging of mutant PFN1 shown in Figure 8.

claim: Cells expressing the ALS-associated G118V disease variant did not associate with actin filaments or microtubules.
source: Cells expressing the ALS-associated G118V disease variant did not associate with actin filaments or microtubules.
evidence: This is supported by live-cell imaging and quantification shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: PFN1 maintains cellular reserves of unassembled actin monomers.
source: It maintains cellular reserves of unassembled actin monomers, catalyzes nucleotide exchange, and sterically inhibits new filament formation (Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1992; Kaiser et al., 1999; Wolven et al., 2000; Suarez et al., 2015; Pimm et al., 2020; Colombo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 catalyzes nucleotide exchange on actin monomers.
source: It maintains cellular reserves of unassembled actin monomers, catalyzes nucleotide exchange, and sterically inhibits new filament formation (Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1992; Kaiser et al., 1999; Wolven et al., 2000; Suarez et al., 2015; Pimm et al., 2020; Colombo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in Figure 3C.

claim: PFN1 sterically inhibits new actin filament formation.
source: It maintains cellular reserves of unassembled actin monomers, catalyzes nucleotide exchange, and sterically inhibits new filament formation (Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1992; Kaiser et al., 1999; Wolven et al., 2000; Suarez et al., 2015; Pimm et al., 2020; Colombo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: PFN1 can drastically stimulate actin assembly when paired with certain PLP-containing ligands (e.g. formins or Ena/VASP).
source: In contrast, PFN1 can drastically stimulate actin assembly when paired with certain PLP-containing ligands (e.g. formins or Ena/VASP) (Manchester, 1998; Romero et al., 2004; Kovar et al., 2006; Breitsprecher and Goode, 2013; Henty-Ridilla and Goode, 2015; Funk et al., 2019; Zweifel and Courtemanche, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Competitive interactions between PFN1, actin monomers, and PIP lipids transmit cellular signals from the plasma membrane to distinct intracellular vesicles.
source: Competitive interactions between PFN1, actin monomers, and PIP lipids transmit cellular signals from the plasma membrane to distinct intracellular vesicles (Lassing and Lindberg, 1985; Davey and Moens, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 directly impacts microtubule organization and polymerization.
source: Furthermore, PFN1 directly impacts microtubule organization and polymerization (Nejedlá et al., 2021; Nejedla et al., 2016; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017; Pimm and Henty-Ridilla, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: Conventional protein tagging strategies using a GFP-derived fluorescent tag on the C- or N-terminus impede PFN1 interactions with PIP lipids or PLP-containing ligands.
source: Conventional protein tagging strategies using a GFP-derived fluorescent tag on the C- or N-terminus impede PFN1 interactions with PIP lipids or PLP-containing ligands (Wittenmayer et al., 2000; Davey and Moens, 2020; Pimm et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Moving the fluorescent tag to a protruding loop in PFN1 restores interactions with PIP lipids and PLP-containing ligands but compromises full actin-binding capacity.
source: Moving the fluorescent tag to a protruding loop in PFN1 restores these interactions, unfortunately compromising full actin-binding capacity (Nejedla et al., 2017; Karlsson and Dráber, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Anti-PFN1 antibodies unambiguously localize PFN1 to stable cytoskeletal structures (i.e. stress fibers, the microtubules, and nuclear components) in cells.
source: This technique unambiguously localizes PFN1 to stable cytoskeletal structures (i.e. stress fibers, the microtubules, and nuclear components) in cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work using immunofluorescence.

claim: Antibody staining of fixed cells obscures the spatiotemporal details required to measure the flux or dynamics of cellular pools of PFN1.
source: However, it obscures the spatiotemporal details required to measure the flux or dynamics of cellular pools of PFN1.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of fixed-cell imaging.

claim: mAp-PFN1 was chosen over standard fluorescent proteins (e.g. GFP) because it is bright, relatively stable, and avoids overlap with the excitation and emission ranges of well-characterized actin-labels used in biochemical assays.
source: We chose the mApple probe over standard fluorescent proteins (e.g. GFP) because it is bright, relatively stable, and avoids overlap with the excitation and emission ranges of well-characterized actin-labels used in biochemical assays (e.g. Oregon-Green; OG, and pyrene-labeled actin; Shaner et al., 2008; Bindels et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations about mApple properties and the experimental design.

claim: The tag-free and tagged versions of PFN1 were of the expected size and highly pure.
source: SDS-PAGE and gel filtration analyses revealed that the tag-free and tagged versions were of the expected size and highly pure (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the SDS-PAGE gel and gel filtration data shown in the figures.

claim: PFN1 binds numerous PIP lipids through two different surfaces that overlap with either the actin- or PLP-binding sites.
source: PFN1 binds numerous PIP lipids through two different surfaces that overlap with either the actin- or PLP-binding sites (Figure 1B; Hartwig et al., 1989; Lambrechts et al., 2002; Skare and Karlsson, 2002; Ferron et al., 2007; Nejedla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural work and the structural diagram in Figure 1B.

claim: PFN1-PI(4,5)P2 interactions inhibit actin polymerization to regulate the morphology of the plasma membrane.
source: PFN1-PI(4,5)P2 interactions inhibit actin polymerization to regulate the morphology of the plasma membrane (Niggli, 2005; Davey and Moens, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1-PI(3,5)P2 interactions facilitate trafficking of late endosomes to the lysosome.
source: In addition, PFN1-PI(3,5)P2 interactions facilitate trafficking of late endosomes to the lysosome (Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1990; Martys et al., 1996; Dong et al., 2000; Hong et al., 2015; De Craene et al., 2017; Hasegawa et al., 2017; Wallroth and Haucke, 2018; Lees et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: mAp-PFN1 and untagged PFN1 were detected bound to either PI(3,5)P2- or PI(4,5)P2-containing liposomes.
source: We detected mAp-PFN1 and untagged PFN1 bound to either PI(3,5)P2- or PI(4,5)P2-containing liposomes via Western blots using PFN1-specific antibodies (Figure 2B-E).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Untagged PFN1 was detected in pellets containing phosphatidylserine (control) or either PI(3,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2 lipids.
source: Untagged PFN1 was detected in pellets containing phosphatidylserine (control) or either PI(3,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2 lipids (Figure 2B-D), but did not pellet without liposomes (buffer alone).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Untagged PFN1 did not pellet without liposomes (buffer alone).
source: Untagged PFN1 was detected in pellets containing phosphatidylserine (control) or either PI(3,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2 lipids (Figure 2B-D), but did not pellet without liposomes (buffer alone).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: mAp-PFN1 binds either PI(3,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2 similar to tag-free PFN1.
source: Blot densitometry confirmed that mAp-PFN1 binds either PI(3,5)P2 or PI(4,5)P2 similar to tag-free PFN1 (Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This is supported by the densitometry quantification shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: PFN1 is a high affinity (kD = 0.1 µM) actin monomer binding protein.
source: PFN1 is a well-characterized, high affinity (kD = 0.1 µM) actin monomer binding protein that catalyzes nucleotide exchange and suppresses actin filament nucleation (Mockrin and Korn, 1980; Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1992; Eads et al., 1998; Vinson et al., 1998; Wolven et al., 2000; Wen et al., 2008; Blanchoin et al., 2014; Colombo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: No change in polarization was detected in reactions that contained untagged PFN1 and OG-labeled actin monomers.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we were unable to detect a change in polarization in reactions that contained untagged PFN1 and OG-labeled actin monomers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Vinson et al., 1998; Kaiser et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations to previous work.

claim: The lack of polarization change with OG-labeled actin is likely due to the short lifetime of the probe.
source: This is likely due to the short lifetime of the probe.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the fluorescent probe.

claim: Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) and PFN1 compete to bind actin monomers.
source: However, several studies demonstrate that Thymosin β4 (Tβ4) and PFN1 compete to bind actin monomers (Goldschmidt-Clermont et al., 1992; Aguda et al., 2006; Xue et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GFP-Tβ4 bound actin with a kD of 5.4 ± 1.2 nM.
source: After confirming that GFP-Tβ4 bound actin (kD = 5.4 ± 1.2 nM; Figure 3A), we used competitive binding assays to measure the affinity of each PFN1 for actin monomers (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PFN1 bound actin monomers with a kD of 99.6 ± 5.1 nM.
source: Each protein bound actin monomers with similar affinity (PFN1: kD = 99.6 ± 5.1 nM or mAp-PFN1: kD = 101.9 ± 6.5 nM; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the competitive fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: mAp-PFN1 bound actin monomers with a kD of 101.9 ± 6.5 nM.
source: Each protein bound actin monomers with similar affinity (PFN1: kD = 99.6 ± 5.1 nM or mAp-PFN1: kD = 101.9 ± 6.5 nM; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the competitive fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The measured kD values are similar to those measured from direct binding assays (kD = 105.2 ± 26.9 nM).
source: These values are similar to those measured from direct binding assays (kD = 105.2 ± 26.9 nM; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B; Wen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the direct binding data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and citation to previous work.

claim: PFN1 catalyzed nucleotide exchange on actin monomers at a rate of k = 18.7 ± 7.5 nM.
source: Each PFN1 catalyzed and accelerated the nucleotide exchange on actin monomers at similar rates (p=0.1; ANOVA) (PFN1: k = 18.7 ± 7.5 nM or mAp-PFN1: k = 13.2 ± 9.7 nM), but were accelerated compared to control reactions lacking either PFN1 (actin alone: k = 514.3 ± 61.6 nM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the time-resolved fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: mAp-PFN1 catalyzed nucleotide exchange on actin monomers at a rate of k = 13.2 ± 9.7 nM.
source: Each PFN1 catalyzed and accelerated the nucleotide exchange on actin monomers at similar rates (p=0.1; ANOVA) (PFN1: k = 18.7 ± 7.5 nM or mAp-PFN1: k = 13.2 ± 9.7 nM), but were accelerated compared to control reactions lacking either PFN1 (actin alone: k = 514.3 ± 61.6 nM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the time-resolved fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Control reactions lacking PFN1 had a nucleotide exchange rate of k = 514.3 ± 61.6 nM.
source: Each PFN1 catalyzed and accelerated the nucleotide exchange on actin monomers at similar rates (p=0.1; ANOVA) (PFN1: k = 18.7 ± 7.5 nM or mAp-PFN1: k = 13.2 ± 9.7 nM), but were accelerated compared to control reactions lacking either PFN1 (actin alone: k = 514.3 ± 61.6 nM) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the time-resolved fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Less total actin polymer was made in the presence of either PFN1 protein compared to the actin alone control.
source: Less total actin polymer was made in the presence of either protein compared to the actin alone control (Figure 3D), demonstrating that both versions of PFN1 inhibit the spontaneous assembly of actin filaments.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk pyrene fluorescence data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both versions of PFN1 inhibit the spontaneous assembly of actin filaments.
source: Less total actin polymer was made in the presence of either protein compared to the actin alone control (Figure 3D), demonstrating that both versions of PFN1 inhibit the spontaneous assembly of actin filaments.
evidence: This is supported by the bulk pyrene fluorescence data shown in Figure 3D and TIRF microscopy data in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Reactions lacking PFN1 (actin alone) had an average of 45.3 ± 1.4 filaments per field of view.
source: Reactions lacking PFN1 (actin alone), had an average of 45.3 ± 1.4 filaments per field of view (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Reactions supplemented with PFN1 had 21.5 ± 3.4 filaments per field of view.
source: In contrast, there were significantly fewer actin filaments in reactions supplemented with either PFN1 (21.5 ± 3.4 filaments) or mAp-PFN1 (19.8 ± 2.9 filaments; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Reactions supplemented with mAp-PFN1 had 19.8 ± 2.9 filaments per field of view.
source: In contrast, there were significantly fewer actin filaments in reactions supplemented with either PFN1 (21.5 ± 3.4 filaments) or mAp-PFN1 (19.8 ± 2.9 filaments; Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Neither PFN1 nor mAp-PFN1 substantially changed the mean elongation rate of actin filaments.
source: As expected, neither protein substantially changed the mean elongation rate of actin filaments (control: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; PFN1: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; mAp-PFN1: 10.05 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Control actin filaments elongated at 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1.
source: As expected, neither protein substantially changed the mean elongation rate of actin filaments (control: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; PFN1: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; mAp-PFN1: 10.05 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Actin filaments in the presence of PFN1 elongated at 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1.
source: As expected, neither protein substantially changed the mean elongation rate of actin filaments (control: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; PFN1: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; mAp-PFN1: 10.05 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Actin filaments in the presence of mAp-PFN1 elongated at 10.05 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1.
source: As expected, neither protein substantially changed the mean elongation rate of actin filaments (control: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; PFN1: 10.07 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; mAp-PFN1: 10.05 ± 0.16 subunits s–1 µM–1; Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: PFN1 is thought to bind to the fast-growing plus-ends of actin filaments at high concentrations (KD >20 µM).
source: PFN1 is thought to bind to the fast-growing plus-ends of actin filaments at high concentrations (KD >20 µM; Jégou et al., 2011; Courtemanche and Pollard, 2013; Pernier et al., 2016; Funk et al., 2019; Zweifel and Courtemanche, 2020; Zweifel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Few (<25 total) transient (>5 s) plus-end localization events of mAp-PFN1 were observed on actin filaments.
source: We observed few (<25 total) transient (>5 s) plus-end localization events (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is supported by the two-color TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: mAp-PFN1 is equivalent to PFN1 for binding to actin monomers, catalyzing nucleotide exchange, and suppressing spontaneous actin assembly.
source: In sum, these data demonstrate that mAp-PFN1 is equivalent to PFN1 for binding to actin monomers, catalyzing nucleotide exchange, and suppressing spontaneous actin assembly.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 3.

claim: Total actin filament polymerization reached similar levels in the presence of PFN1 or mAp-PFN1.
source: Total actin filament polymerization reached similar levels in the presence of PFN1 or mAp-PFN1 (Figures 3D and 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk pyrene fluorescence data shown in Figures 3D and 4A.

claim: Actin filaments assembled with the constitutively active formin mDia1(FH1-C) and either protein resulted in a strong enhancement in actin polymerization.
source: Actin filaments assembled with the constitutively active formin mDia1(FH1-C) and either protein resulted in a strong enhancement in actin polymerization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the bulk pyrene fluorescence data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: TIRF reactions containing actin and mDia1(FH1-C) had an average of 659.3 ± 98.3 filaments.
source: TIRF reactions containing actin and mDia1(FH1-C) had an average of 659.3 ± 98.3 filaments, which was significantly higher (p=0.014, ANOVA) than control reactions lacking formin or either PFN1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Reactions containing formin and tag-free PFN1 had 42.7 ± 9.8 filaments.
source: Consistent with previous reports that PFN1 also suppresses formin nucleation, reactions containing formin and either tag-free (42.7 ± 9.8 filaments) or mAp-PFN1 (48.3 ± 14.5 filaments) had statistically fewer filaments than control reactions containing formin and actin (p=0.0004, ANOVA) (Kovar et al., 2006; Breitsprecher et al., 2012; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and citations to previous work.

claim: Reactions containing formin and mAp-PFN1 had 48.3 ± 14.5 filaments.
source: Consistent with previous reports that PFN1 also suppresses formin nucleation, reactions containing formin and either tag-free (42.7 ± 9.8 filaments) or mAp-PFN1 (48.3 ± 14.5 filaments) had statistically fewer filaments than control reactions containing formin and actin (p=0.0004, ANOVA) (Kovar et al., 2006; Breitsprecher et al., 2012; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 suppresses formin nucleation.
source: Consistent with previous reports that PFN1 also suppresses formin nucleation, reactions containing formin and either tag-free (42.7 ± 9.8 filaments) or mAp-PFN1 (48.3 ± 14.5 filaments) had statistically fewer filaments than control reactions containing formin and actin (p=0.0004, ANOVA) (Kovar et al., 2006; Breitsprecher et al., 2012; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and citations to previous work.

claim: Actin filaments elongated at two different speeds that correspond to unassisted growth (10.1 ± 0.4 subunits s–1 µM–1) and mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted growth in the presence of PFN1.
source: We measured actin filaments elongating at two different speeds that correspond to the recorded rates of unassisted growth (10.1 ± 0.4 subunits s–1 µM–1) and mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted growth in the presence of PFN1 (PFN1: 42.7 ± 9.8 subunits s–1 µM–1; or mAp-PFN1: 48.3 ± 14.5 subunits s–1 µM–1) (Kovar et al., 2006; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous work.

claim: mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted actin filament growth in the presence of PFN1 occurred at 42.7 ± 9.8 subunits s–1 µM–1.
source: We measured actin filaments elongating at two different speeds that correspond to the recorded rates of unassisted growth (10.1 ± 0.4 subunits s–1 µM–1) and mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted growth in the presence of PFN1 (PFN1: 42.7 ± 9.8 subunits s–1 µM–1; or mAp-PFN1: 48.3 ± 14.5 subunits s–1 µM–1) (Kovar et al., 2006; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous work.

claim: mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted actin filament growth in the presence of mAp-PFN1 occurred at 48.3 ± 14.5 subunits s–1 µM–1.
source: We measured actin filaments elongating at two different speeds that correspond to the recorded rates of unassisted growth (10.1 ± 0.4 subunits s–1 µM–1) and mDia1(FH1-C)-assisted growth in the presence of PFN1 (PFN1: 42.7 ± 9.8 subunits s–1 µM–1; or mAp-PFN1: 48.3 ± 14.5 subunits s–1 µM–1) (Kovar et al., 2006; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 4E and citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 and mAp-PFN1 stimulate formin-based actin assembly to comparable levels.
source: These data demonstrate that PFN1 and mAp-PFN1 stimulate formin-based actin assembly to comparable levels.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: Microtubules in control reactions polymerized at an average rate of 1.9 ± 0.2 µm–1 min–1.
source: Microtubules in control reactions polymerized at an average rate of 1.9 ± 0.2 µm–1 min–1 (Figure 5B–C), whereas microtubules polymerized in the presence of either PFN1 grew at rates ~6 fold faster (PFN1: 12.7 ± 0.3 µm–1 min–1; mAp-PFN1: 12.6 ± 0.4 µm–1 min–1; Figure 5B, C; p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Microtubules polymerized in the presence of PFN1 grew at rates of 12.7 ± 0.3 µm–1 min–1.
source: Microtubules in control reactions polymerized at an average rate of 1.9 ± 0.2 µm–1 min–1 (Figure 5B–C), whereas microtubules polymerized in the presence of either PFN1 grew at rates ~6 fold faster (PFN1: 12.7 ± 0.3 µm–1 min–1; mAp-PFN1: 12.6 ± 0.4 µm–1 min–1; Figure 5B, C; p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Microtubules polymerized in the presence of mAp-PFN1 grew at rates of 12.6 ± 0.4 µm–1 min–1.
source: Microtubules in control reactions polymerized at an average rate of 1.9 ± 0.2 µm–1 min–1 (Figure 5B–C), whereas microtubules polymerized in the presence of either PFN1 grew at rates ~6 fold faster (PFN1: 12.7 ± 0.3 µm–1 min–1; mAp-PFN1: 12.6 ± 0.4 µm–1 min–1; Figure 5B, C; p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Reactions performed in the presence of either PFN1 had significantly longer microtubules.
source: Consistent with elevated microtubule growth rates, reactions performed in the presence of either PFN1 had significantly longer microtubules (Figure 5D; p<0.0001, ANOVA) that displayed more stable growth behaviors (Figure 5E; p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Microtubules in the presence of either PFN1 displayed more stable growth behaviors.
source: Consistent with elevated microtubule growth rates, reactions performed in the presence of either PFN1 had significantly longer microtubules (Figure 5D; p<0.0001, ANOVA) that displayed more stable growth behaviors (Figure 5E; p<0.0001, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Reactions containing either PFN1 had more microtubules than controls.
source: Reactions containing either PFN1 had more microtubules than controls (Figure 5F; p=0.0048, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: mAp-PFN1 binds unlabeled tubulin dimers with a kD of 1.89 ± 0.28 µM.
source: To test for a direct interaction between mAp-PFN1 and unlabeled tubulin dimers, we performed fluorescence polarization (kD = 1.89 ± 0.28 µM) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence polarization data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The affinity of mAp-PFN1 for tubulin dimers is 5.9-fold stronger than its affinity for polymerized microtubules (kD = ~10 µM).
source: This affinity is 5.9-fold stronger than its affinity for polymerized microtubules (kD = ~10 µM) (Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to a previously published value.

claim: mAp-PFN1 localized to the side of growing microtubules rather than decorating plus-ends.
source: Rather than decorating plus-ends, mAp-PFN1 localized to the side of growing microtubules (Figure 5H–I and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: Side-bound mAp-PFN1 molecules appear to diffuse along the microtubule lattice.
source: Side-bound mAp-PFN1 molecules appear to diffuse along the microtubule lattice (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: mAp-PFN1 and PFN1 are equivalent regulators of microtubule dynamics.
source: Thus, mAp-PFN1 and PFN1 are equivalent regulators of microtubule dynamics, and promote assembly by direct interactions with dimers and the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: mAp-PFN1 and PFN1 promote microtubule assembly by direct interactions with dimers and the microtubule lattice.
source: Thus, mAp-PFN1 and PFN1 are equivalent regulators of microtubule dynamics, and promote assembly by direct interactions with dimers and the microtubule lattice.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Mutations in PFN1 are associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Mutations in PFN1 are associated with neurodegenerative disease, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS; Wu et al., 2012; Murk et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Two clonal CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines (PFN1(-/-)) were generated in immortalized neuroblastoma-2a (N2a) cells.
source: Therefore, we generated and confirmed two clonal CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines (PFN1(-/-)) in immortalized neuroblastoma-2a (N2a) cells (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C) that have been successfully used to model features of ALS (De Vos, 2007; Vance et al., 2009; Coussee et al., 2011; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: N2a cells have been successfully used to model features of ALS.
source: Therefore, we generated and confirmed two clonal CRISPR/Cas9 knockout lines (PFN1(-/-)) in immortalized neuroblastoma-2a (N2a) cells (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C) that have been successfully used to model features of ALS (De Vos, 2007; Vance et al., 2009; Coussee et al., 2011; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 deficient cell lines did not proliferate as efficiently as endogenous controls.
source: PFN1 deficient cell lines did not proliferate as efficiently as endogenous controls (Figure 6B), consistent with previously reported cell cycle defects (Suetsugu et al., 1998; Witke et al., 2001; Moens and Coumans, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6B and citations to previous work.

claim: N2a cells contain 121 ± 15 µM PFN1.
source: N2a cells contain 121 ± 15 µM PFN1 and each plasmid harboring tagged or tag-free PFN1 restored the protein to endogenous levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Each plasmid harboring tagged or tag-free PFN1 restored the protein to endogenous levels.
source: N2a cells contain 121 ± 15 µM PFN1 and each plasmid harboring tagged or tag-free PFN1 restored the protein to endogenous levels (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PFN1(-/-) knockout cell morphology significantly deviated from all cells expressing PFN1 (endogenous, tagged, or untagged).
source: PFN1(-/-) knockout cell morphology significantly deviated from all cells expressing PFN1 (endogenous, tagged, or untagged; p=0.01; ANOVA; Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the cell morphology data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Knockout cells displayed strikingly aberrant actin filament networks.
source: In addition, knockout cells displayed strikingly aberrant actin filament (p=0.02; ANOVA; Figure 6G and H) and microtubule networks (p=0.002; ANOVA; Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claim: Knockout cells displayed strikingly aberrant microtubule networks.
source: In addition, knockout cells displayed strikingly aberrant actin filament (p=0.02; ANOVA; Figure 6G and H) and microtubule networks (p=0.002; ANOVA; Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claim: The cell morphology, architecture of actin filaments, and shape of the microtubule network was not different between PFN1(+/+) and PFN1(-/-) cells expressing tag-free or mAp-PFN1 plasmids.
source: Compared to PFN1(+/+), the cell morphology, architecture of actin filaments, and shape of the microtubule network was not different than PFN1(-/-) cells expressing tag-free or mAp-PFN1 plasmids (p=0.78; ANOVA; Figure 6E and J and Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: mAp-PFN1 complements cytoskeleton-based activities in cells.
source: This demonstrates that mAp-PFN1 complements cytoskeleton-based activities in cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 6.

claim: Eight mutations in PFN1 cause ALS.
source: Eight mutations in PFN1 cause ALS (Wu et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1(G118V) is an ALS variant that does not effectively bind actin monomers or microtubules.
source: Empowered by the knowledge that mAp-PFN1 fully compensates for PFN1, we measured cell and cytoskeletal morphology parameters for PFN1(-/-) cells expressing Halo-PFN1(G118V), an ALS variant that does not effectively bind actin monomers or microtubules, (Figure 7; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PFN1 deficient cells displayed aberrant cell morphology.
source: Consistent with analyses comparing cells expressing mAp-PFN1 (Figure 6E–J), PFN1 deficient cells displayed aberrant cell morphology (p=0.02; ANOVA; Figure 7A and B), as well as significantly decreased fluorescence of actin filaments (p=0.03; ANOVA; Figure 7C and D) and microtubules (p=0.01; ANOVA; Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: PFN1 deficient cells displayed significantly decreased fluorescence of actin filaments.
source: Consistent with analyses comparing cells expressing mAp-PFN1 (Figure 6E–J), PFN1 deficient cells displayed aberrant cell morphology (p=0.02; ANOVA; Figure 7A and B), as well as significantly decreased fluorescence of actin filaments (p=0.03; ANOVA; Figure 7C and D) and microtubules (p=0.01; ANOVA; Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7C and D.

claim: PFN1 deficient cells displayed significantly decreased fluorescence of microtubules.
source: Consistent with analyses comparing cells expressing mAp-PFN1 (Figure 6E–J), PFN1 deficient cells displayed aberrant cell morphology (p=0.02; ANOVA; Figure 7A and B), as well as significantly decreased fluorescence of actin filaments (p=0.03; ANOVA; Figure 7C and D) and microtubules (p=0.01; ANOVA; Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: PFN1(-/-) cells expressing only Halo-PFN1(G118V) were unable to compensate for cell morphology, actin filament, or microtubule defects.
source: PFN1(-/-) cells expressing only Halo-PFN1(G118V) were unable to compensate for any of these parameters (p=0.01; ANOVA; Figure 7A–F).
evidence: This is supported by the imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claim: PFN1(G118V) contributes to ALS through actin and microtubule-based mechanisms.
source: Thus, PFN1(G118V) contributes to ALS through actin and microtubule-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The endogenous protein is present at high cellular concentrations (121 µM).
source: The discrete cellular localization of PFN1 has been difficult to determine because the endogenous protein is present at high cellular concentrations (121 µM; Figure 6D; Pollard et al., 2000; Funk et al., 2019; Skruber et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative Western blot data shown in Figure 6D and citations to previous work.

claim: At high concentrations of JF-646, Halo-PFN1 was localized to the nucleus and throughout the cytoplasm.
source: At high concentrations of JF-646, Halo-PFN1 was localized to the nucleus and throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Single molecules of Halo-PFN1 were identified at 1–10 nM ligand.
source: Single molecules of Halo-PFN1 were identified at 1–10 nM ligand, and localized to microtubules in ~60% of N2a cells (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: Halo-PFN1 localized to microtubules in ~60% of N2a cells at 1-10 nM JF-646 ligand.
source: Single molecules of Halo-PFN1 were identified at 1–10 nM ligand, and localized to microtubules in ~60% of N2a cells (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8A-C.

claim: In NIH 3T3 cells, Halo-PFN1 localized to actin filaments in all cells assessed.
source: In NIH 3T3 cells, Halo-PFN1 localized to actin filaments in all cells assessed and only occurred with microtubules at sites where both polymers overlapped (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: In NIH 3T3 cells, Halo-PFN1 only occurred with microtubules at sites where both actin and microtubules overlapped.
source: In NIH 3T3 cells, Halo-PFN1 localized to actin filaments in all cells assessed and only occurred with microtubules at sites where both polymers overlapped (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Halo-PFN1 associated more frequently with microtubules than actin filaments for U2OS and N2a cells.
source: In contrast, Halo-PFN1 associated more frequently with microtubules than actin filaments for U2OS and N2a cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: For N2a cells, the localization of Halo-PFN1 to actin filaments only occurred at sites where both actin and microtubules overlapped.
source: Notably, for N2a cells, the localization of Halo-PFN1 to actin filaments only occurred at sites where both polymers overlapped (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Expressing Halo-PFN1 over endogenous PFN1 did not stimulate further microtubule association.
source: Expressing Halo-PFN1 over endogenous PFN1 did not stimulate further microtubule association (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PFN1 colocalized with microtubules in >50% of cells expressing the actin monomer binding deficient PFN1, Halo-PFN1(R88E).
source: PFN1 colocalized with microtubules >50% of cells expressing the actin monomer binding deficient PFN1, Halo-PFN1(R88E) (n>50 cells from 5 separate experiments; Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8B-C.

claim: PFN1 colocalized with microtubules in >75% of cells expressing the formin/poly-L-proline binding deficient Y6D mutation.
source: Surprisingly, PFN1 colocalized with microtubules in >75% of cells expressing the formin/poly-L-proline binding deficient Y6D mutation (Figure 8B and C; Ezezika et al., 2009; Henty-Ridilla et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8B and C and citations to previous work.

claim: Microtubules in cells expressing Y6D appear less dynamic than wild-type or R88E-expressing cells.
source: Microtubules in these cells appear less dynamic than wild-type or R88E-expressing cells, which may strengthen the hypothesis that PFN1-microtubule interactions stabilize microtubule dynamics (Figure 8D and Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: PFN1-microtubule interactions may stabilize microtubule dynamics.
source: Microtubules in these cells appear less dynamic than wild-type or R88E-expressing cells, which may strengthen the hypothesis that PFN1-microtubule interactions stabilize microtubule dynamics (Figure 8D and Figure 8—video 1).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of less dynamic microtubules.

claim: Significantly less PFN1 was associated with microtubules in cells expressing the microtubule-binding deficient, and ALS-relevant, G118V mutation.
source: Significantly less PFN1 was associated with microtubules in cells expressing the microtubule-binding deficient, and ALS-relevant, G118V mutation (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: Cells expressing G118V displayed PFN1 accumulations that may be disease-relevant aggregates hypothesized to contribute to ALS onset.
source: These cells displayed PFN1 accumulations may be disease-relevant aggregates that are hypothesized to contribute to ALS onset (Wu et al., 2012; Figley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The localization of molecules of PFN1 can be shifted from actin- or microtubule-binding activities with specific point mutations.
source: Thus, the localization of molecules of PFN1 can be shifted from actin- or microtubule-binding activities with specific point mutations.
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the data in Figure 8.
